{"artifact":"SmeDossierEnvelope","schema_version":"0.4.0","stage_id":"02.dossier_sections","probe":"rdmv-nj-d","lineage":{"input_manifest_sha256":"55fbe4883b85f1e7c473e53d5e3d8b04004ba3238884cdca2eb899e04cb58c25","candidate_lineage_id":"2026-10-28-rdmv-nj-class-d:lineage:19","source_registry_sha256":"057b72c7c679c997f56ae00ef97a6b14dbe264551f4121b9bf67b0457d9cf7c1","source_liveness_sha256":"1ca7bfbb9e3c0a6b19e5e808ecab6fe8329f3b4799e394abc260d65c1d6513e7"},"envelope_scope":{"kind":"partial_chunk","assigned_section_ids":["C"],"chunk_index":1,"chunk_total":1},"section_char_limit":12000,"sections":[{"section_id":"C","chunk_id":"C.01","merge_seq":1,"domain":"Vehicle control: steering, stopping, signals, reversing, turning and parking","heading":"C — Vehicle control: steering grip, stopping distances, proper braking, signals, driving in reverse, turning, the K-turn and parking","learner_facing":true,"markdown":"## C — Vehicle control: steering grip, stopping distances, proper braking, signals, driving in reverse, turning, the K-turn and parking
Knowledge domain: the basic vehicle-control skills a New Jersey driver is expected to know and show — where to hold the steering wheel, what stopping distance depends on, how to brake, which turn and hand signals to give, how to back up, how to plan a turn and make a K-turn, and how to park on hills, in angle spaces and parallel to the curb.

FACT_ID: sec05-F01 | anchor: A01
For normal driving, hold the outside rim of the steering wheel at the 9 and 3 o'clock positions, with your thumbs resting along the face of the wheel. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec05-F02 | anchor: A01
Holding the wheel at those positions lowers the risk of hand, wrist or arm injury if the air bag deploys. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec05-F03 | anchor: A01
Never turn the steering wheel while holding it from the inside of the rim with your hand facing inward. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec05-F04 | anchor: A01
Both hands should stay on the wheel at all times except while shifting gears or giving hand signals. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec05-F05 | anchor: A01
Keep the vehicle centered in its lane, and on a two-lane road with oncoming traffic stay to the right. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec05-F06 | anchor: A01
When steering hand-over-hand through a turn, the hands may travel as much as 165 degrees around the wheel. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec05-F07 | anchor: A02
Hand-over-hand steering works especially well for precision maneuvers, curves, entering and leaving intersections, and recovering from a skid. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0054]

FACT_ID: sec05-F08 | anchor: A02
Stopping distance depends on the driver's reaction time, weather and visibility, vehicle weight, brake condition, tire type and condition, the road surface and speed. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0054]

FACT_ID: sec05-F09 | anchor: A02
One rule always holds: the faster a vehicle is moving, the longer it needs to stop. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0054]

FACT_ID: sec05-F10 | anchor: A03
At 60 mph a vehicle covers 88 feet every second. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec05-F11 | anchor: A03
Under most traffic conditions, a typical driver's reaction time is three-quarters of a second. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec05-F12 | anchor: A03
The manual's stopping table gives a total of 53 feet at 20 mph, made up of 22 feet of reaction distance and 31 feet of braking distance. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec05-F13 | anchor: A03
The manual's stopping table gives a total of 247 feet at 50 mph, made up of 55 feet of reaction distance and 192 feet of braking distance. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec05-F14 | anchor: A03
Slamming the brake pedal when there is no emergency is a common new-driver mistake that jerks the car to a stop and wears out brakes and tires; steady, gentle pressure gives a controlled stop. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec05-F15 | anchor: A03
A vehicle with anti-lock brakes may lose control at only 35 mph, even on dry pavement, if the driver brakes while violently jerking the steering wheel. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec05-F16 | anchor: A03
Use the right foot for both the brake and the gas pedal; with a manual transmission, the left foot works only the clutch. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec05-F17 | anchor: A04
Give a proper signal whenever you turn, change lanes, stop or slow down. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec05-F18 | anchor: A04
Switch on the turn signal at least 100 feet before turning, and cancel it after the turn so other drivers are not misled. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec05-F19 | anchor: A04
The hand signal for stopping or slowing down is the arm extended downward with the palm facing the rear. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec05-F20 | anchor: A04
The hand signal for a right turn is the arm extended upward. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec05-F21 | anchor: A04
The hand signal for a left turn is the arm held straight out. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec05-F22 | anchor: A04
A driver may sound the horn when passing another vehicle outside a business or residential zone. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec05-F23 | anchor: A04
Under normal conditions a horn must be audible from at least 200 feet away. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec05-F24 | anchor: A04
Sirens, whistles and bells are reserved for emergency vehicles. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec05-F25 | anchor: A04
In reverse, turning the wheel to the right sends the vehicle to the right, turning it left sends it left, and holding it straight backs the vehicle straight. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec05-F26 | anchor: A05
To back up in a straight line, turn your head and body to the right so you can see out the back window without mirrors, rest your right arm over the front passenger seat, and hold the top of the wheel with your left hand. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0057]

FACT_ID: sec05-F27 | anchor: A05
Back up slowly, usually at walking speed of 2 to 4 mph. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0057]

FACT_ID: sec05-F28 | anchor: A05
Do not shift into a forward gear until the vehicle has come to a complete stop. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0057]

FACT_ID: sec05-F29 | anchor: A05
Steering with one palm while turning in reverse is dangerous and can make an applicant fail the road test; use both hands while looking out the rear window. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0057]

FACT_ID: sec05-F30 | anchor: A05
On the road test the applicant backs the vehicle about 100 feet in a straight line, slowly and smoothly. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0057]

FACT_ID: sec05-F31 | anchor: A05
Since August 31, 2016, backup cameras and parking sensors installed on a vehicle may be used during the road test, but the basic reversing principles still come first. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0057]

FACT_ID: sec05-F32 | anchor: A05
If you miss a turn, never back up; taking the next turn is safer than risking a crash. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0057]

FACT_ID: sec05-F33 | anchor: A06
Before turning, check your mirrors behind and to both sides, and look for less visible road users such as motorcycles, bicycles and mopeds. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0058]

FACT_ID: sec05-F34 | anchor: A06
Signal first, with the turn signal or a hand signal, and only then move into the proper lane for the turn. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0058]

FACT_ID: sec05-F35 | anchor: A06
Stay in the same lane until the turn is complete, then make sure the turn signal has switched off. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0058]

FACT_ID: sec05-F36 | anchor: A06
To turn around, start at the right edge of the road at a safe spot where you can see well in both directions. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0058]

FACT_ID: sec05-F37 | anchor: A06
In a K-turn, signal left and pull forward turning left to stop several inches from the left curb or street edge, back up turning right to stop several inches from the right curb or edge, then pull forward turning left and straighten the wheels. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0058]

FACT_ID: sec05-F38 | anchor: A06
A new driver is required to make the 3-point turn, also called the K-turn, during the MVC road test. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0058]

FACT_ID: sec05-F39 | anchor: A07
Whenever you park, set the brake and put the vehicle in park, or for a manual transmission in reverse or low gear. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0059]

FACT_ID: sec05-F40 | anchor: A07
When parking downhill next to a curb, set the hand brake and turn the wheels toward the curb, with a manual transmission left in reverse. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0059]

FACT_ID: sec05-F41 | anchor: A07
When parking uphill next to a curb, set the hand brake and turn the wheels away from the curb, with a manual transmission left in low. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0059]

FACT_ID: sec05-F42 | anchor: A07
When backing out of an angle space, tap the horn to warn nearby pedestrians, and once you can see past the tops of the neighboring vehicles, stop and look again. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0059]

FACT_ID: sec05-F43 | anchor: A08
An applicant must be able to parallel park to pass the MVC road test, and it is the maneuver that needs the most practice. [A08]
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0060]

FACT_ID: sec05-F44 | anchor: A08
To practice parallel parking, set out flags or markers 25 feet apart; hitting them means you are not ready to park between real vehicles. [A08]
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0060]

FACT_ID: sec05-F45 | anchor: A08
To start parallel parking, pull up alongside the vehicle in front, about two to four feet away from it. [A08]
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0060]

FACT_ID: sec05-F46 | anchor: A08
A properly parallel-parked vehicle has its tires no more than six inches from the curb. [A08]
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0060]

Misconceptions: a missed turn is never fixed by backing up; front-wheel or rear-wheel drive does not change how to brake; a backup camera may be used on the road test but the basic reversing principles still come first; the right-turn hand signal is the arm up, not out.
Mnemonics: hands at nine and three; downhill means wheels toward the curb, uphill means wheels away from it; signal a hundred feet ahead; back up at walking speed.
Glossary: hand-over-hand steering means turning by crossing one hand over the other while both stay on the wheel; controlled slipping means letting the wheel slide through the fingers to straighten after a turn; reaction distance and braking distance mean the two parts of the manual stopping table that add up to the total stopping distance; K-turn means the three-point turn used to reverse direction on a street.
Dynamic facts: road test equipment rules, such as the allowance for backup cameras and parking sensors, can change; confirm them on the MVC website before a road test.
